I don't have a recommendation for a single bible, but I've got a single recommendation for multiple bibles.

LOTS of choices. I'm going to go in a bit of a different direction: Byzantine text-type (NKJV is more eclectic): Meaning the majority of manuscripts, dating from much later than the Critical text. Whether this is good or bad really depends on your viewpoint.

  1. KJV: Accurate, but old, difficult to read and understand if you don't "get" old English. Also has some difficult syntax.

  2. NKJV: Like the KJV, but modernized. It is, however, a NEW translation, so don't let someone tell you that it's an "update." the Preface denies that.

Critical Text: People who translated from this text type are your typical modern scholars, most of them quite good at what they do. In this group, my personal favorite is the NASB, but see my notes on that version. The critical text DOES "leave things out," but their reasoning is that because these passages were not in the text THEY are translating from, the passages were never in the original, and added later. However, many modern versions have added them back because of the outcry against their exclusion (John 7:53-8:11 and Mark 16, at the end, are the two strongest examples). The fact that they have been added back argues for one of two things: either the translators and publishers are spineless wusses, or they SHOULDN'T have been excluded in the first place, which also calls into question the whole theory of textual criticism.

  1. NIV: Popular version, but very often paraphrases difficult passages. Most recent revision full of political correctness (gender neutrality).

  2. NLT (New Living Translation): Very much a paraphrase. Nice to have as a commentary, but not really ok to read as your "only Bible," even though it's very easy to understand.

  3. ESV: Claims to be a "new" translation, but my reading tells me it's essentially an update of the old RSV. It IS a good version,

  4. NASB: Literal translation (sometimes a real weakness, especially in Paul's letters; syntax can sometimes be messed up); very conservative, carefully done.

  5. HCSB: Attempts to be a "new" translation; translated for Holman & Co., very popular among Southern Baptists (they were a major force in the translation). There are lots of others, and you should investigate them for yourself. There is not really THAT much difference between them for the nontechnical person, except in the way they put things, EXCEPT for the NIV. Despite its popularity, the NIV does attempt "gender neutrality." After much thought, I have to oppose this, because of the fact that it is changing the text in favor of a political position. I've got strong feelings about that, most of them summarized in the words, "What else might they change later?"

My Personal Favorites: KJV, NASB, NKJV, in that order. Even though the NASB is built off the critical text, it's carefully done, very mature, and modern, despite its defects (reading is somewhat more difficult than some others). I like the literalness.
